entry.title: Major League Baseball’s New Salary Cap Proposal Is As Shady As Its Old One
entry.summary: In the lead-up to an inevitable springtime lockout, Major League Baseball has revised the salary cap-and-floor plan it first proposed back in July. The significance of these details is different from sports leagues that already have salary caps, where the numbers are the point. In MLB the fight concerns whether a salary cap will exist at all, with ownership offering up version after version of what a cap could resemble, and players ostensibly declining, baseball bat in hand, until the basic yes-or-no question has been answered. The latest version, proposed by MLB on Nov. 3, would delay the implementation of a cap from 2027 to 2028. This is less a concession to players than it is to teams, giving them a full offseason to prepare rather than launching into a cap system immediately after a lockout. The new numbers offered by MLB are projections, contingent on league revenue, which presumably will change dramatically in '27 depending on the duration of the lockout. To simplify, the proposed projected cap would sit at $258.2 million, and the floor at $180.2 million, or at about 70 percent of the cap. This would, in theory, work out to players receiving a 50-50 percent split of league revenue. But like all cap systems, the finer details are contingent on how revenue is collected and how spending is defined.

entry.title: Irreal: A New Journelly Beta
entry.summary:
Journelly. I use it as my memo book to record my daily activities and random things that I want to remember. For example, if I see some article or ad in my browser, I can ask Safari to share it with Journelly and a Journelly entry is automatically made complete with a link to whatever it was I wanted to capture. Each entry contains a date/time stamp as well as the location of where the entry was made.
Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.
I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.
If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.

entry.title: If You’re Going To Change Your School’s Mascot, At Least Have The Decency To Get Weird
entry.summary: The University of San Francisco is a staid enclave of higher learning, a rectangular hodgepodge of buildings gerrymandered to fill 19 square blocks of prime city real estate. It is a culturally and ethnically diverse educational operation and has been so for decades. Also, it has no football team to interfere with the peace and quiet of the place, and its men's basketball team has not been of national consequence in 45 years. In other words, it minds its business. So far, so good. So it came as a bit of a jar when the school decided last Friday to change its mascot from a cartoon Spanish don—his name is Don Francisco, and he has both the requisite outsized biceps and a jaunty pencil-thin mustache of the kind last worn by Ronald Colman seven decades ago—to a wolf, an animal which is not particularly indigenous to any part of the city, save maybe the Financial District. Even then they could have just gone with Rapacious Bastards and sold a few more T-shirts when they roll out the new mascot next spring. It has taken four years to implement this move, which began with a student government proposal to ditch the mascot in 2022. That became a petition signed by approximately 400 students, who correctly viewed the mascot as a representation of the Spanish colonization/brutalization of the indigenous population four centuries ago. All good, there; the student body should be the deciding vote on anything on campus that impacts mostly students. It's their house, after all.

entry.title: Irreal: Ridenour On Literate Calc Mode
entry.summary:
another step in the journey so many of are on: moving everything inside Emacs. Regular Irreal readers will recall that Ridenour is a Philosophy professor so he doesn’t have much need for high powered math tools but he does have to deal with grade calculations and various budget items. He had been using Soulver for this but, of course, this meant leaving Emacs, something all we Emacers hate.
Then he stumbled on literate-calc-mode. It did everything that Soulver did and Ridenour didn’t have to leave Emacs to use it. It’s been a win for him and he’s happy with it.
When I read Ridenour’s post, something seemed familiar. It turns out that I’d written about literate-calc-mode six years ago. It had just been released and no one had any experience with it yet. I meant to follow up but, of course, life intervened and I never did. I’m glad to see that it’s still around and has lived up to its potential.
I’m tempted to install it but I’m reasonably proficient with Calc itself so I probably wouldn’t use it enough to make it worthwhile. Still, if Reverse Polish Notation is not your thing and you’d rather deal with normal infix notation, literate-calc-mode may be a good fit. It’s easy to try out so give it a spin if you’re interested.

entry.title: Randy Ridenour: Emacs Literate Calc Mode
entry.summary:
Soulver on the Mac.
I recently stumbled on Literate Calc Mode by Robin1 that does everything I was using Soulver for, and I now have one more reason to not leave Emacs. It’s in Melpa, so installing it is simple. Once required, it provides both literate-calc-mode and literate-calc-minor-mode. I find the minor mode particularly useful for Org mode scratch buffers. For example, I used it recently to sketch out some details for a conference funding request. In an Org buffer, I entered:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 Parking = 10 Registration = 295 Mileage = 300 Meals = 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals
M-x literate-calc-minor-mode instantly changed it to this:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 => Hotel: 500 Parking = 10 => Parking: 10 Registration = 295 => Registration: 295 Mileage = 300 => Mileage: 300 Meals = 200 => Meals: 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals => Total: 1,305
=> is not editable and displayed in a lighter shade. Changing one of the variable values results in an instant update of the total. It uses Calc, so it is able to do almost anything that Calc can do. So far, I’ve used it to plan travel expenses and to build material lists for woodworking projects. It works flawlessly and I’ve found it surprisingly useful to have a scratchpad that can automatically do the math.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing mdired, or adding a chainsaw to Dired
entry.summary: The ability to mark items in GNU Emacs Dired allows for bulk operations on both files and directories. With marking, onerous tasks can be turned into a trivial ones. While default Dired has many bulk operation commands, not everything is covered. That is the motivation for mdired, an Elisp package which extends Dired with some SIMD-style commands. Using these commands fall into two steps: Mark the items of interest in Dired. Run the mdired command. mdired supports the following four commands: mdired-copy: copy a single file to multiple directories. mdired-do-command: run an Elisp command or named keyboard macro on multiple files. mdired-compile: run compile on multiple directories. mdired-byte-recompile: byte-compile selected files or directories. Refer to the mdired User Guide for more details on usage. Closing Thoughts Bulk operation commands are chainsaws. Use them with caution. That said, they are great for improvised workflows: “Here’s this file that I want copied to a bunch of directories.” “I want to do the same edit operation on this set of files. I’ve got a named keyboard macro ready to go on them.” “I want to run the same make command on a bunch of directories.” As mdired is new, I’m open to feedback on it. Let me know what you think. mdired v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

entry.title: Irreal: Highlighting The Active Window
entry.summary:
marking the active window (update here ) so that it’s easy to pick it out from the other, inactive windows. I did that by making the mode line of the active window a distinct color instead of the slightly different shade of gray from the other windows. That’s worked out really well for me and I’ve never looked back.
Now Ray Zeitler over at Ray on Emacs takes another look at the problem and found a really nice solution. It’s a bit more in your face than mine so if you’re looking for something that makes the active window really stand out, you should take a look at his post. The TL;DR is that instead of changing the active window, he changes the background color of all the other windows.
Zeitler found his solution on a 10 year old Stack Exchange post so it’s pretty certain to work no matter what version of Emacs you’re using. The code is very simple and you can simply copy it to your init.el if you’re interested.
As I said, this solution seems a little aggressive to me so I doubt I’ll be implementing it but others may disagree. One thing for sure, it’s going to make your active window stand out. It’s a small enough change that you can try it out—say by copying it to your scratch buffer and executing it—to see if it’s something you’d like.

I will keep the chat open, in case there are any questions related to this or anything else—I always answer everything. About Denote Denote is a simple note-taking tool for Emacs. It is based on the idea that notes should follow a predictable and descriptive file-naming scheme. The file name must offer a clear indication of what the note is about, without reference to any other metadata. Denote basically streamlines the creation of such files while providing facilities to link between them. Denote’s file-naming scheme is not limited to “notes”. entry.title: Irreal: Emacs Turns 50
entry.summary:
MIT Technology Review there’s a nice article on Emacs turning 50 this year. It gives a short history of Emacs starting from its TECO days. Most of that history is pretty well known to seasoned Emacs users but it’s still interesting.
What the article doesn’t give is the exact day of Emacs’ 50th birthday. That’s not surprising. The early history of Emacs involved the researchers at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory agreeing on a standard set of TECO macros in order to improve collaboration. That was undoubtedly an ongoing process that didn’t have a well defined beginning or end so it’s easy to understand why the exact birthday of Emacs is a little murky.
Regardless, we can all celebrate Emacs’ 50th year. It’s remarkable when you think about it. Very few programs last that long. There’s FORTRAN and Lisp, of course, but I can’t think of any other piece of software with that sort of longevity. There is, to be sure, a Ship of Theseus aspect to that longevity but it’s one shared by FORTRAN and Lisp as well.
Who knows what things will look like in another 50 years but if we still have editors, I’m putting my money on Emacs still being around. Wouldn’t that be something?

entry.title: Irreal: Electric Quote Mode
entry.summary:
Unicode punctuation in Emacs. His post is mainly concerned with the vagaries of dealing with English and Polish punctuation in the same document but a lot of the heavy lifting is accomplished with Electric Quote Mode.
The main problem is handling single and double quotes ‘like this’ and “like this”. Because I do almost all my writing in Org mode, I use the ':t option to turn the ASCII double quote (") into their curved typeset equivalents on export. That’s supposed to do the same with single quotes but I could never get it to work for me and always had to add then manually.
Fortunately, it’s easy to make everything work right in the buffer as you type. You merely turn electric-quote-mode on and it takes care of everything for you. By default it acts the way TeX used to by requiring “ for an opening double quote and ” for the closing double quote and similarly for single quotes. You can make it accept ” and ‘ instead by setting electric-quote-replace-double and electric-quote-context-sensitive to t.
Electric Quote Mode is global so turning it on enables it for all your buffers. You can use electric-quote-local-mode if you want it only in the current buffer. You can toggle either of them on or off by simply calling Meta+x electric-quote....
If you have to deal different quote notation for two or more languages, take a look at mbork’s post for a nifty solution.

entry.title: Irreal: Controlling Where Isearch Starts Searching
entry.summary:
new Emacs trick from Emacs Dwelling. Well, new to me. It turns out it’s been in Emacs since 28.1 so for about four and a half years.
Here’s the problem. When you call isearch it starts searching at the current point location to the bottom of the file. You can cause it to wrap around and continue searching at the top of the file but this isn’t always convenient. As a result, many people always start their search by moving to the top of the buffer first. But this isn’t always convenient either. For example, if you quit the search you go back to the top of the file, not where you started.
Sometimes you want a bit more control: perhaps you want to start at the first match or the last match and if you quit, you’d like to be back where you started. Well this is Emacs so of course you can do that. The nice thing is that it’s already built in. There are no packages to install, you just enable it my setting isearch-allow-motion to t.
You can start the search at any of:
The current point position The first match in the file The last match in the file The first match before the window The first match after the window
